newsitem.title: UK: UK's Ofwat warns firms on investment plans.
newsitem.headline: UK's Ofwat warns firms on investment plans.

text.p: UK water industry watchdog Ofwat said that companies which had "materially changed the phasing of their capital programmes" compared with planning should not raise prices to the full allowable extent next April.
In a statement, Ofwat head Ian Byatt said "I do not believe that they should take up their full price limit next April."
The statement was made with the publication of Ofwat's Report on Financial Performance and Capital Investment for 1995-96, published on Tuesday.

Ofwat said many companies had shown they could become more efficient and improve services while reducing operating expenditure in real terms and these cost cuts could be passed on to customers at the next price review in 1999.
"The companies' capital expenditure is also less than Ofwat had expected when it set price limits in 1994," Ofwat added.
Under Ofwat regulation, price rises are limited to a formula linked to the retail price index to keep them below inflation.
Ofwat said the financial report gave early indications of financial trends and "some of these are giving concern."
Companies are being asked to report on progress to Byatt.
"There is no question of reverting to the undesirable practices of the past when capital expenditure was controlled on an annual basis by the Treasury," Ofwat said.
But it added that "we must make sure that there is no slippage in (company) performance which is critical to customers."
"These are serious issues which I am currently exploring with the companies concerned and with the quality regulators," Byatt said.
The report said capital investment by the water and sewerage companies in the core business totalled 2.6 billion stg in 1995-96 compared with 1.6 billion stg in the 1980s.
Operating costs are down while current cost profits after interest but before tax for the water utilities were 1.8 billion stg in 1995-96, "more or less static after rising since privatisation."
At the same time, Ofwat said, dividend payouts have risen sharply, up 22 percent in 1995-96 over a year earlier to 1.6 billion stg.

"Unless there are very good reasons, I do not approve of dividend payments from the regulated business to the parent group which are in excess of what is needed to meet the cost of capital," Byatt said. They should distribute a "proper share" of efficiency benefits to shareholders, he said.

He said that licence conditions covering multi-utilities Hyder and United Utilities requiring them to set out a dividend policy to comply with written requirements might have to be extended to cover other firms where "compliance with existing licence conditions is perfunctory."
